data.name: United Kingdom
data.summary: High-tax for a long-term resident: 24% CGT, 39.35% top dividend rate (from April 2026), 40% inheritance tax on worldwide assets after 10 years of residence, no wealth tax. New arrivals get a 4-year exemption for foreign income and gains (FIG regime) and stay outside IHT on foreign assets for about 10 years. No investor visa route. A family investment company pays 25% on gains but nothing on most dividends, with dividend tax (up to 39.35%) or tax-free loan repayments on extraction, and lets future growth pass to the children outside IHT.

regimes.name: Ordinary UK tax residence
regimes.description: Arising-basis taxation of worldwide income and gains for UK residents under the Statutory Residence Test. The remittance basis and domicile concept were abolished from 6 April 2025.
regimes.eligibility: UK tax resident under the Statutory Residence Test (183+ days, only home in the UK, or sufficient ties). Requires a visa for all except British and Irish citizens.

capital_gains.summary: UK residents pay CGT on worldwide gains. From 6 April 2025 (unchanged for 2026/27) the rates are 18% within the basic-rate band and 24% above it, for shares and residential property alike. A large gain for a wealthy investor is taxed at 24%. Annual exempt amount £3,000.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Annual exempt amount £3,000 (individuals). Main home exempt under private residence relief. Gains inside ISAs (£20,000/year subscription) and on UK government gilts and qualifying corporate bonds are exempt. Business Asset Disposal Relief and Investors' Relief: 18% from 6 April 2026 (14% in 2025/26), on up to £1m lifetime gains each.
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: Applies to individuals resident under the Statutory Residence Test.
capital_gains.regional_differences: CGT is UK-wide; Scottish income tax bands do not change CGT rates (the band test uses UK bands).
capital_gains.important_exceptions: No CGT uplift on lifetime gifts: a gift to a child is a disposal at market value (holdover relief only for business assets/trusts). Death gives a CGT-free uplift to market value. Temporary non-residence: gains realised abroad within 5 years of leaving can be taxed on return. Carried interest moved wholly into income tax from 6 April 2026.

capital_gains.rate_basis: Higher/additional-rate taxpayer rate of 24% (2026/27) on all asset types including residential property. Private business sale shown at 24%; the first £1m of lifetime qualifying gains under BADR is taxed at 18% (2026/27), which barely changes the rate on a large sale.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Frequent dealing can be treated as a trade (badges of trade) and taxed as income at up to 45% plus National Insurance. A long-term investor holding a diversified portfolio is normally within CGT.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: No holding period reduces the rate. BADR needs a 2-year qualifying period (5% shareholding and employee/officer of a trading company).
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Worldwide gains taxed on the arising basis (remittance basis abolished from 6 April 2025). Foreign tax on the gain is creditable.

dividends.summary: Dividends above a £500 allowance are taxed at 10.75% (basic), 35.75% (higher) and 39.35% (additional rate, income above £125,140) from 6 April 2026. Budget 2025 raised the two lower rates by 2 points; the 39.35% top rate is unchanged. A wealthy family pays 39.35% at the margin on UK and foreign dividends.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: £500 dividend allowance. Dividends inside ISAs are exempt. Personal allowance (£12,570) withdrawn between £100,000 and £125,140.
dividends.regional_differences: Dividend rates are UK-wide (Scotland's own rates apply only to non-savings, non-dividend income).
dividends.important_exceptions: Interest income (relevant for bonds) is taxed at 20/40/45% in 2026/27, rising to 22/42/47% from 6 April 2027 (savings rates increase announced in Budget 2025). Offshore funds without reporting status: gains taxed as income (up to 45%).

From April 2028 a High Value Council Tax Surcharge applies in England to homes worth £2m+ (2026 valuation): £2,500 (£2-2.5m), £3,500 (£2.5-3.5m), £5,000 (£3.5-5m), £7,500 (£5m+), CPI-indexed from 2029-30; announced, design consulted on in 2026, not yet in force. inheritance.summary: Inheritance tax (IHT) of 40% on the estate above a £325,000 nil-rate band (frozen to April 2031). Since 6 April 2025 scope depends on residence, not domicile: a 'long-term UK resident' (UK resident in at least 10 of the previous 20 tax years) is taxed on worldwide assets; others only on UK-situs assets. Children are not exempt.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: Nil-rate band £325,000 per person; the first spouse's unused band passes to the survivor (IHTA 1984 s.8A), so £650,000 at the second death when everything went to the spouse first, the case modelled here (as both exclusions are counted for the US). Residence nil-rate band £175,000 for a home left to children, withdrawn by £1 per £2 above a £2m estate (so nil for a wealthy family). Spouse exemption unlimited between two long-term residents (capped at £325,000 to a non-long-term-resident spouse). Annual gift exemption £3,000; regular gifts from surplus income exempt without limit.
inheritance.eligibility_conditions: Applies to deaths and transfers on or after 6 April 2025 under the long-term residence rules (IHTA 1984 ss.6A-6C).
inheritance.important_exceptions: Business Property Relief / Agricultural Property Relief: from 6 April 2026 100% relief is capped at a combined £2.5m per person (raised from the £1m first announced; unused allowance transferable to a spouse, so up to £5m), 50% relief above it. Shares on non-'listed' markets such as AIM get only 50% relief (effective 20% IHT). Unused pension funds and most pension death benefits come into the estate from 6 April 2027 (Finance Act 2026). Excluded-property trusts largely lose protection under the new rules.

open_questions: The app's single rate cannot show that a newly arrived family's non-UK assets fall outside IHT for roughly their first 10 years of residence; scored here as the long-term-resident position.
inheritance.spouse_note: Transfers to a spouse or civil partner are exempt without limit (Inheritance Tax Act 1984 s. 18(1)), but where the transferor is a long-term UK resident and the spouse is not, the exemption is capped at the exemption limit, £325,000 (s. 18(2)); the gift must not be conditional beyond 12 months or take effect after an interest ends (s. 18(3)). It defers rather than removes the tax: the assets form part of the survivor's estate.
inheritance.gift_tax: No gift tax on outright gifts to individuals (potentially exempt transfers). If the donor dies within 7 years, the gift is brought back into charge (40%, tapered: 32% at 3-4 years, 24% at 4-5, 16% at 5-6, 8% at 6-7). Gifts into most trusts are chargeable immediately at 20% above the nil-rate band.
inheritance.business_relief: BPR 100% on unlisted trading company shares and business interests up to £2.5m (combined with APR) per person from 6 April 2026, 50% above; 50% on AIM shares and controlling holdings of listed companies; investment-holding businesses excluded; 2-year ownership. Any unused part of the £2.5m allowance transfers to a surviving spouse or civil partner (GOV.UK, page updated 3 March 2026; the allowance was raised from the £1m first announced).
inheritance.foreign_assets: Long-term UK residents: worldwide estate. Non-long-term residents: UK-situs assets only (including UK shares, UK property and, through look-through rules, UK residential property held via companies).
inheritance.domicile_rules: Long-term UK resident = UK resident for at least 10 of the previous 20 tax years (s.6A IHTA 1984, from 6 April 2025). Tail after leaving: 3 years for 10-13 years of residence, rising by one year per extra year to 10 years for 20 years of residence. Ten consecutive non-resident years reset the count. Under-20s have modified rules (s.6B). Probate fee £526 for estates over £5,000 (negligible).

regimes.name: 4-year foreign income and gains (FIG) regime
regimes.description: Replaced the remittance basis from 6 April 2025. New arrivals who were non-UK resident for at least 10 consecutive tax years can claim, in each of their first 4 tax years of UK residence, that foreign income and gains are not taxed in the UK, whether or not brought into the UK. Claims cost the personal allowance and CGT annual exempt amount.
regimes.eligibility: First 4 tax years of UK residence after at least 10 consecutive tax years of non-residence; annual claim; available regardless of nationality or domicile. Foreign employment income is excluded (Overseas Workday Relief may apply). Temporary Repatriation Facility (12% in 2025/26-2026/27, 15% in 2027/28) is only for pre-April-2025 income of former remittance-basis users.

capital_gains.summary: For a qualifying new arrival who claims the 4-year FIG regime, foreign capital gains are not taxed in the UK in tax years 1-4 of residence, and can be brought into the UK freely. UK gains (UK shares, UK property) stay taxable at 24%. Claimants lose the £3,000 CGT annual exempt amount.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Foreign gains claimed under the regime are exempt. No CGT annual exempt amount and no income-tax personal allowance in a year of claim.
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: UK tax resident and within the first 4 tax years of residence after at least 10 consecutive tax years of non-UK residence. Claim made each year in the self-assessment return; sources can be chosen; unused years cannot be carried forward; years of temporary non-residence cannot be claimed.
capital_gains.regional_differences: CGT is UK-wide; Scottish income tax bands do not change CGT rates (the band test uses UK bands).
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Foreign gains on assets sold after year 4 are taxed in full (no rebasing for the regime). Gains realised in the 4 years are exempt even if the money is remitted. Being away for 10 consecutive years is needed before a new 4-year period can start.

regimes.name: Family investment company (FIC, private limited company)
regimes.description: The parents fund a UK private company, usually with a loan plus a small subscription, and the company holds the portfolio. It pays 25% corporation tax on gains (one point more than personal CGT at 24%) and on interest, but most dividends it receives are exempt, against 39.35% personally. Money comes out as dividends at 10.75% / 35.75% / 39.35%, or tax-free as repayment of the parents' loan. The main reason families use a FIC is inheritance tax: children hold growth or non-voting 'alphabet' shares, so future growth accrues outside the parents' estates while the parents keep control. IHT itself (40%) is unchanged on whatever the parents still own; the inheritance metric is inherited from the standard regime. For a newly arrived family the 4-year FIG regime and the 10-year IHT exclusion of foreign assets are usually better in the early years: FIC shares are UK-situs assets and are within IHT from day one.
regimes.eligibility: Any UK resident can incorporate a company (Companies House). Works for a passive investor family. US citizens are excluded: a UK company with US shareholders is a CFC/PFIC for US tax, so its passive income is taxed in the US currently.
regimes.duration_note: Ordinary corporation-tax rules with no time limit; the company lasts as long as the family keeps it.

structure.entity: Family investment company (private company limited by shares)
structure.payout_notes: Dividends to UK-resident individuals are taxed at 10.75% (basic), 35.75% (higher) and 39.35% (additional rate, income above GBP 125,140) in 2026/27, after a GBP 500 allowance; 0.3935 assumes the parents are additional-rate taxpayers. Dividends can be steered to adult children or a spouse with lower bands through alphabet share classes (settlements legislation applies to minor children of the settlor and to bounty). The usual design funds the company with an interest-free loan from the parents repayable on demand: repaying the loan returns capital free of personal tax, so in practice withdrawals of GBP 400k a year can be tax-free for many years (the loan stays in the parents' estates for IHT). Salaries are subject to income tax and NIC.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: No small profits rate (close investment-holding company). No business property relief for IHT: shares in a company whose business is wholly or mainly making or holding investments are not relevant business property (IHTA 1984 s.105(3)). Anti-avoidance to plan around: settlements legislation (ITTOIA 2005 Part 5 Chapter 5), transactions in securities (ITA 2007 s.684), gifts with reservation of benefit, IHTA s.98 on altering share rights, and s.3(3) IHTA if dividend rights are not exercised. Funds put into a FIC are not potentially exempt transfers in themselves; gifts of shares to children are PETs (40% IHT falls away after 7 years). HMRC's earlier review of FICs found no link to non-compliance but HMRC has not ruled out future challenges (ICAEW). Annual accounts and a corporation tax return are required; audit is usually not needed for a small company.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: On liquidation, distributions are capital for the shareholders and taxed at 24% CGT (no Business Asset Disposal Relief for an investment company; the TAAR in ITTOIA s.396B can tax them as dividends if the activity continues). The company stays UK-resident if the family emigrates (UK has no exit tax on individuals); dividends to non-residents bear no UK withholding, but the 5-year temporary non-residence rule taxes close-company distributions received while abroad on return. Moving central management abroad would trigger a corporate exit charge. IHT: growth/freezer share structures shift future growth to children; FIC shares (UK-situs) remain in the IHT net even for non-long-term residents.

capital_gains.summary: Gains realised by the company are taxed at the 25% main corporation tax rate. A FIC is normally a close investment-holding company, so it cannot use the 19% small profits rate or marginal relief. No indexation for assets acquired from 1 January 2018. The substantial shareholding exemption needs a 10% stake in a trading company, so portfolio gains are fully taxable. Real estate gains are also taxed at 25%.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: No annual exempt amount for companies. Substantial shareholding exemption: 10%+ holdings in trading companies/groups.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Funding the FIC with existing shares is a disposal at market value by the parents (connected parties), taxed at 24%; FICs are therefore usually funded with cash. A gain-standing portfolio inside a FIC gets no uplift on the parents' death (only the FIC shares are revalued).

income_tax.summary: For 2026/27 (England, Wales and Northern Ireland) UK income tax is 0% up to a GBP 12,570 personal allowance, 20% to GBP 50,270, 40% to GBP 125,140 and 45% above, with an effective 60% rate between GBP 100,000 and GBP 125,140 as the allowance is withdrawn. Employee National Insurance is 8% between GBP 12,570 and GBP 50,270 and 2% above; self-employed Class 4 is 6% and 2%. Scotland has its own rates (not modelled).
income_tax.self_employed_notes: Class 4 NIC 6% on profits between GBP 12,570 and GBP 50,270 and 2% above (PwC gives 2025/26 'and onwards'); Class 2 abolished from April 2024 (voluntary GBP 3.50 a week). The nomad persona would pay about 6% on most of the profit.
income_tax.local_tax_note: Brackets are on gross income with the GBP 12,570 allowance built in (0% band), so the personal allowance field is 0; the 60% band reproduces the taper (allowance lost GBP 1 per GBP 2 above GBP 100,000). Thresholds frozen until at least April 2031. NIC: 8% on GBP 12,570-50,270, then 2% on everything above - modelled as 8% with a cap of GBP 50,270, ignoring the 2% above. Employer NIC (15%) not counted. No local income tax in London.

regimes.name: 4-year foreign income and gains (FIG) regime
regimes.description: New UK residents who were non-UK resident for the previous ten tax years can claim exemption on qualifying foreign income and gains during their first four years of UK residence, regardless of domicile. It does NOT cover UK employment income or UK-source earnings; those are taxed at the ordinary rates above. Overseas workday relief for employment duties performed abroad is capped at the lesser of GBP 300,000 or 30% of qualifying employment income a year for eligible FIG individuals (cap not applied to those arriving in 2023/24 or 2024/25).

Applies to a nomad earning from foreign clients only if the work is performed outside the UK; UK-performed self-employment income is taxed normally.

income.residence_routes: The UK has no digital nomad visa; the GOV.UK work-visa list contains none for remote workers. EU citizens no longer have free movement and, like US and other nationals, need a visa. Skilled employees use a Skilled Worker visa with a sponsor (general minimum GBP 41,700 or the occupation going rate, whichever is higher, for applications since 22 July 2025). Without a job offer, Global Talent and High Potential Individual routes exist. Self-employed non-UK nationals have no general route (Innovator Founder only).

succession.name: United Kingdom
succession.summary: England and Wales and Northern Ireland have no forced heirship, but a court can order provision for close family. Scotland protects spouse and children with legal rights over movable estate. Trusts are fully recognised; there is no private foundation.
succession.family_claims: England and Wales: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975; Northern Ireland: 1979 Order. Scotland instead has fixed legal rights: spouse and children each take 1/3 (with both) or 1/2 of the movable estate, Succession (Scotland) Act 1964 ss. 8-10.
succession.foreign_law_note: Movables follow the law of the deceased's domicile (which can stay foreign), immovables follow the law of their location. Nationality is irrelevant and there is no choice of law as such.
succession.trust_note: Hague Trusts Convention in force for the UK since 1 January 1992. Trusts are taxed: 20% entry charge above the nil-rate band, 6% every ten years on relevant property. No private foundation form; charitable incorporated organisations exist.
open_questions: Current rates of trust and inheritance tax were not rechecked.

Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

assumptions: The family has been non-UK resident for at least 10 consecutive tax years, so it can claim the 4-year foreign income and gains regime in years 1-4. It stays UK resident after that.

Dividends are taxed at the additional rate throughout: with EUR 600,000 a year of dividends, even if shared between the spouses, each is far above GBP 125,140. The dividend allowance and the CGT annual exempt amount are ignored.

Long-term residence (10 of the last 20 tax years) is reached in year 10, so at both deaths in the model the worldwide estate is within UK inheritance tax. During years 1-9 only UK-situs assets would be, which the fig_4_year regime records but no death falls in that period.

The family investment company is funded with cash, or with shares whose cost is today's value. Transferring existing low-cost shares is a disposal at market value (TCGA 1992 s.17): foreign gains would be tax-free in a FIG year but taxed at 24% afterwards.
Payout from the company is modelled at 39.35% in the tax file (additional-rate dividends). The usual interest-free loan repaid tax-free is not modelled.
open_questions: Needs an engine change: a family investment company is normally funded by an interest-free loan from the parents; repaying that loan is not income, so withdrawals of GBP 400,000 a year are free of personal tax until the loan is repaid, and only then are dividends taxed at up to 39.35% (ITA 2007 s.8). The engine applies the 39.35% payout rate from year 1; it needs a payout path that starts tax-free up to the loan balance.

Needs an engine change: lifetime gifts. A gift to children is a potentially exempt transfer, free of inheritance tax if the donor survives 7 years, with taper relief between years 3 and 7 (IHTA 1984 s.3A, s.7(4)). The engine has taxable events only at the two deaths, so the standard UK planning (gifts and gift of FIC growth shares) cannot be shown.

Needs an engine change: contributing shares to the family investment company during the 4 FIG years is a disposal whose foreign gain is exempt under the claim (TCGA 1992 s.17 with the FIG exemption), giving the company a market-value base tax-free. The engine has no asset-transfer event.

Needs an engine change: the 40% inheritance-tax charge applies to the estate of each parent, and the nil-rate band and (tapered) residence band of the first parent to die transfer to the survivor (IHTA 1984 s.8A); the engine taxes a single estate at a death.

Tax file: the family_investment_company structure records no annual running cost (accounts, corporation tax return, administration), unlike the Italian holding S.r.l.; the check therefore counts none. Typical costs of a few thousand pounds a year would matter little at this size.
The legislation section for the FIG regime was not read in the Finance Act 2025 text; the check rests on HMRC's guidance on the 4-year regime.

paths.name: Holding the portfolio personally (ordinary residence)
paths.note: Dividends at the additional rate of 39.35% with credit for foreign withholding, gains at 24%, no wealth tax. Inheritance tax on the worldwide estate at 40% above the GBP 325,000 nil-rate band once long-term resident.

paths.name: 4-year foreign income and gains regime, then ordinary residence
paths.note: In the first 4 tax years of residence (after 10 consecutive years of non-residence) a claim leaves foreign dividends and foreign gains outside UK tax. From year 5 the ordinary rules apply. The family becomes long-term resident after 10 tax years, so at both deaths (years 30 and 60) inheritance tax covers the worldwide estate.

paths.name: Family investment company
paths.regime: Family investment company (FIC, private limited company)
paths.note: A UK company owns the portfolio: corporation tax at 25% on gains, foreign dividends exempt (CTA 2009 Part 9A). The parents' estate holds the company shares: a company that holds investments gets no business property relief (IHTA 1984 s.105(3)), so inheritance tax is the same as for personal holding.

immigration.name: United Kingdom
immigration.summary: EU free movement ended on 31 December 2020: EU citizens now need a visa like everyone else, except those who joined the EU Settlement Scheme (deadline 30 June 2021) and Irish citizens, who live in the UK freely under the Common Travel Area. There is no investor visa (Tier 1 Investor closed on 17 February 2022) and no digital nomad visa. The routes open to most people are Innovator Founder (an endorsed business, settlement after 3 years), Global Talent (endorsed leaders in research, arts and digital technology) and Skilled Worker (a sponsored job paying at least GBP 41,700).
immigration.naturalisation: British citizenship usually after 5 years of residence, with indefinite leave to remain (ILR) held for 12 months first. A government plan to move the settlement baseline to 10 years ('earned settlement') was consulted on in late 2025 and was not in the Immigration Rules as of mid-2026; check before relying on 5 years. A higher English standard (B2) for several settlement routes is announced for 26 March 2027.
immigration.dual_citizenship_note: The UK does not require renouncing another nationality (not stated on the GOV.UK page fetched; widely known, no official source cited here).

routes.name: Common Travel Area (Irish citizens)
routes.summary: Irish citizens can live, work and study in the UK without a visa. Only Irish citizens benefit, not other EU citizens.
routes.requirements: Irish citizens 'can move freely and reside in' the UK under the Common Travel Area; no registration or minimum period is stated on the GOV.UK page. Other EU citizens are not covered.
routes.tax_note: Tax residence follows the Statutory Residence Test.

routes.name: EU Settlement Scheme (settled / pre-settled status)
routes.status_note: Deadline for most people was 30 June 2021; only joining family members of those resident by 31 December 2020 and certain reapplicants can still apply (GOV.UK, accessed 16 October 2026).
routes.summary: EU citizens who lived in the UK before the end of 2020 could apply for status; for almost everyone new the scheme is closed.
routes.requirements: Residence in the UK by 31 December 2020; settled status after 5 years in a row; applying is free. Pre-settled status is extended by 5 years before expiry. Not a route for someone arriving today.
routes.physical_presence: Continuous residence; status can lapse after long absence

routes.name: Innovator Founder visa
routes.summary: For people starting a new, innovative business endorsed by an approved body. No fixed investment amount is stated on GOV.UK; settlement is possible after 3 years.
routes.requirements: Business must be new, innovative, viable with growth potential and scalable, endorsed by an approved endorsing body; English language; endorsement fee GBP 1,000 and at least two meetings with the endorsing body at GBP 500 each (12 and 24 months). Reported personal funds GBP 1,270 held for 28 days and English B2 (secondary source, not on the GOV.UK page fetched). Initial stay up to 3 years, extendable by 3 years without limit. EU citizens (except Irish) need this visa like anyone else.
routes.fees_note: GBP 1,357 applying from outside the UK (GBP 1,693 inside) plus GBP 1,000 endorsement and the immigration health surcharge.
routes.physical_presence: Live in the UK; settlement requires limited absences (allowed days not sourced)
routes.family: Partner and children can apply as dependants.
routes.tax_note: Becoming tax resident depends on the Statutory Residence Test.

routes.name: Global Talent visa
routes.summary: For recognised or potential leaders in academia and research, arts and culture, or digital technology; no job offer is needed. Up to 5 years at a time.
routes.requirements: Be 18 or over and a leader or potential leader in the field; either win an eligible prize or get endorsement from the designated body for the field. Stay up to 5 years, extendable in 1 to 5 year steps. Settlement after 3 or 5 years depending on field and route.
routes.fees_note: GBP 766 in total (GBP 561 endorsement + GBP 205 visa, or GBP 766 on the prize route); immigration health surcharge about GBP 1,035 a year.
routes.physical_presence: Live in the UK; absence limits for settlement not sourced
routes.processing_time: About 3 weeks outside the UK, 8 weeks inside
routes.family: Partner and children each pay GBP 766.

routes.name: Skilled Worker visa
routes.summary: A sponsored job on the eligible occupations list. The general salary floor is GBP 41,700 a year or the occupation's going rate, whichever is higher.
routes.requirements: Job offer from a licensed sponsor on the eligible list, minimum salary GBP 41,700 a year or the going rate (GBP 33,400 in some cases), English. Up to 5 years before extending; settlement after 5 years.
routes.physical_presence: Live and work in the UK
